--- NONFICTION_caa4e5dc92.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L31
The things we fear tend to attract us, don't they? Although I have been known to drink too much and will probably do so again, what I fear most is losing control of my words, my thoughts, my life. One reason I like H. P. Lovecraft's work so much is because that fear is central to so many of his tales. His critics may find fault with it, but I think "The Thing on the Doorstep" is his scariest story. The ghouls who infest The Throne of Bones have the power to possess the personalities of the corpses they eat -- often to the point where the "subsumed" persons believe they are still alive and acting normally. That idea scares me. Madness, disease, addiction, imprisonment -- all of these can take control of you. Death, of course, is the ultimate manipulator. It's always fascinated me, but I can't say I fear it. Unlike some of the people in my tales, I don't expect to know it when I'm dead. You might say I try to make death a bit scarier than it really is. Ed Bryant and others identify you as a horror writer from way back. Do you think of yourself as a horror writer now?

[2] Ghouls L55
As for the model of my world, I used ours, through the looking-glass. Gibbon's vision of the Roman Empire was a strong influence, but I didn't overlook the world around me. When Vendriel the Good observes that the suspicion of madness in a ruler is never an obstacle to good government, I was thinking of Richard Nixon's flair for foreign policy. Why zombies? What in particular made you want to use them as the horror trope at the center of The Throne of Bones? Not zombies, dammnit, ghouls! In Voodoo, a zombie is a resurrected corpse. There are a few of those in Throne, but I never call them that, since the word carries associative baggage from that belief and, more recently, from all the books and movies spawned by Night of the Living Dead. [3] Ghouls L55
Why zombies? What in particular made you want to use them as the horror trope at the center of The Throne of Bones? Not zombies, dammnit, ghouls! In Voodoo, a zombie is a resurrected corpse. There are a few of those in Throne, but I never call them that, since the word carries associative baggage from that belief and, more recently, from all the books and movies spawned by Night of the Living Dead. In Arabic myth, ghouls are spirits that haunt graveyards, where they eat the bodies of the dead and sometimes of the living. Their credentials as "spirits" are questionable, though. In the Arabian Nights, their appetite for food is equaled by their appetite for sex. Since the conditions of their existence have never been set in granite -- as those of vampires and werewolves have been, for instance -- I felt free to invent those conditions. Is The Throne of Bones substantially different from your other writing? If so, why in particular? Those stories are set in another world, where society is more rigidly structured and where magic is a part of life.

[4] Ghouls L67
"The Retrograde Necromancer" is one of my personal favorites from the collection. It's one of the most clever dark fantasies I've read in quite awhile. Would you care to comment on how you came to write it? And what is your own personal favorite in the collection? I set out to write a story about something else entirely, one that determinedly refused to be written. "The Retrograde Necromancer" just sort of popped out of my head while I wasn't looking. I'm very fond of "Meryphillia," which my old friend Gene DeWeese described as a Romeo and Juliet for ghouls. That's just what I had in mind when I wrote it. The dust jacket for the book includes an appreciation by the publisher, Ken Abner. He mentions you have a whole chronology and set of maps for Seelura. You didn't want these published with the collection. Abner mentions those items as "crutches." Could you elaborate on why you didn't want the chronology and maps published? None of that stuff is really finished -- and if it were, I would feel less inclined to write fiction about my imaginary world.

[5] Ghoul L85
What process do you go through in editing and revising your rough drafts? If I were marooned on a desert island, I suspect I would write in the sand with a stick. I have written in longhand when other means were unavailable, but I greatly prefer a computer. I revise and cut and rearrange exhaustively, and a computer is well suited to that method. There is an interesting tension in your stories, I feel, between the physicality of the world and the spirituality of the world. On the one hand, you slop blood and guts all over the place (a somewhat necessary side effect of using ghoul characters) and on the other, you have a touching delicacy with regard to human emotion -- I'm thinking, for example, of the end of "Reunion in Cephalune," in particular these sentences about the zombies: "Those who dared creep close enough descried a curiously domestic scene on its portico; a young man and woman who sat very still as they observed, day after day, the interplay of light and shadow across the desert." Would you comment on this tension -- and am I right in thinking that you sometimes worry about maintaining the right balance? I believe that we are soft creatures in a world with some very hard edges. It's remarkable that we survive at all, much less do high deeds or write great music. I think the tension you speak of is a condition of our existence, and I do my best to depict it. Why do you think the bottom has fallen out of the horror market?

--- Nephren-Ka.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L97
P. Lovecraft Nephren-Ka "The Black Pharaoh" (also called Nophru-Ka ) is a fictional pharaoh of Ancient Egypt. The character was originally created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story " The Outsider ", depicted as being a worshipper of the Outer God Nyarlathotep . Later versions of the Cthulhu Mythos presented him as an avatar of Nyarlathotep himself. In Lovecraft's Fiction Lovecraft first mentioned Nephren-Ka in the short story " The Outsider " (written in March-August 1921, and published in April 1926), whose narrator says near the story's close: Now I ride with the mocking and friendly ghouls on the night-wind, and play by day amongst the catacombs of Nephren-Ka in the sealed and unknown valley of Hadoth by the Nile. I know that light is not for me, save that of the moon over the rock tombs of Neb, nor any gaiety save the unnamed feasts of Nitokris beneath the Great Pyramid.... Nephren-Ka is alluded to briefly in The Case of Charles Dexter Ward (1927/1941), in which necromancer Edward Hutchinson signs one of his letters, "Nephren-Ka nai Hadoth, Edw. H." This seems to be some sort of invocation; his colleague Simon Orne signed a letter " Yogg-Sothoth Neblod Zin, Simon O."

Similarly, " The Colour Out of Space " refers to "farms, ancient and rocky, with squat, moss-coated cottages brooding eternally over old New England secrets". "Cool Air" Season Two's 12th episode, first aired December 8, 1971, led with an adaptation of H. P. Lovecraft's " Cool Air ", directed by Jeannot Szwarc from a teleplay by Rod Serling. It starred Henry Darrow as Dr. Juan Muñoz; Barbara Rush as Agatha Howard, a friend and potential love interest of Muñoz; and Beatrice Kay as Mrs. Gibbons, Muñoz's housekeeper. Director Szwarc commented: As it is written, Lovecraft is impossible to adapt because you can never find a visual equivalent of his style.

[1] Ghoul L47
НАЗВАНИЕ: Nightmares of Lovecraft ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:26:24 СИМВОЛОВ: 770 Nightmares of Lovecraft Country United States Genre(s) Action figures Collectible statues Publisher SOTA Toys Release Date October 2006 Nightmares of Lovecraft is an American toyline originally released by SOTA Toys in October 2006. It was set for release in 2005, before ultimately getting delayed. The figures are based on familiar entities from the Cthulhu Mythos , ranging in the 7-inch to 10-inch scale with multiple points of articulation. The first wave consists of Cthulhu from " The Call of Cthulhu ", the Ghoul from " Pickman's Model ", and Dagon from The Shadow Over Innsmouth The line also featured some collectible statues, including a 14-inch Ultra Cthulhu Statue released in June 2008, and a 12-inch polystone statue of Nyarlathotep released in late 2009.

НАЗВАНИЕ: Nitokris ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:26:27 СИМВОЛОВ: 3834 Nitokris Origin Ancient Egypt Powers and Abilities Immortality Occupation Pharaoh Species Human First appearance HPL Imprisoned with the Pharaohs Created by H. P. Lovecraft Nitokris or Nitocris was a possibly historical queen of Ancient Egypt , who may have ruled at the end of the 6th Dynasty, from 2184—2181 BC. H. P. Lovecraft incorporated her legend into the Cthulhu Mythos , referring to her as the "ghoul-queen". ( HPL Imprisoned with the Pharaohs Nitocris' historicity is today debated, but she was considered to be real by ancient historians like Manetho, who (wrongly) attributed the building of the Third Pyramid at Giza to her, and Herodotus, who presents her as the avenger of her brother, whom she succeeded on the throne: He had been the king of Egypt, and he had been put to death by his subjects, who then placed her upon the throne.

[2] Ghouls L97
That is all I know about her. It was not only easier but more amusing to imagine her character and all the names of her enemies than to be bothered with reading about her. In Lovecraft's Fiction Lovecraft first mentioned Nitokris in his story " The Outsider ," written in 1921 and first published in 1926. The piece refers to "the unnamed feasts of Nitokris beneath the Great Pyramid," in a passage that also evokes the "catacombs of Nephren-Ka " and "the mocking and friendly ghouls on the night-wind." Nitokris comes up repeatedly in " Under the Pyramids ," which was ghostwritten for Harry Houdini in 1924 and published that same year.

[3] Ghoul L117
It invokes both the legend of her drowning her enemies and her connection to the Third Pyramid: Even the smallest of them held a hint of the ghastly—for was it not in this that they had buried Queen Nitokris alive in the Sixth Dynasty; subtle Queen Nitokris, who once invited all her enemies to a feast in a temple below the Nile, and drowned them by opening the water-gates? I recalled that the Arabs whisper things about Nitokris, and shun the Third Pyramid at certain phases of the moon. The story also links Nitokris to the Pharaoh Khephren , telling of rumors that he "lives far underground wedded to the ghoul-queen Nitokris and ruling over the mummies that are neither of man nor of beast Toward the end of the story, the narrator Houdini actually sees the "beautiful Queen Nitokris," and notices that "the right half of her face was eaten away by rats or other ghouls." In Expanded Mythos Works In " The Mirror of Nitocris Brian Lumley depicts Nitocris as reviving the worship of Nyarlathotep , uncovering the Shining Trapezohedron , and possessing a magical mirror that functioned similarly to the Trapezohedron. In Demonbane , the Mirror of Nitocris was one of the missing fragments of the Necronomicon . It has the power to break the boundaries between reality and fiction. Nya gave it to Allison, who used it to summon the creatures from Wonderland Haiyore!

[1] Ghouls L39

Nanjo Takenori's "A Night at Yuan-Su" was also not so much Mythos centered, but definitely Lovecraftian, with echoes of "The Outsider" and "He," as well as classic Japanese ghost stories. "Summoned by the Shadows" by Hirayama Yumeaki is a sort of Mythos version of Rosemary's Baby, and its a frightening and imaginative tale to boot! In addition to the fine fiction displayed within, we also have an article on Lovecraftian role-playing games in Japan, and Bob Price is in especially fine, and even quite jocular form, with his Introduction, "Cults of the Ghouls," which takes a long-overdue look at the various types of Mythos cultists and dissects their seemingly mad motivations! So, all in all, a wonderful book, especially worthwhile for the Price introduction, and the stories "The Horror in the Kabuki Theater," "Taste of Snake's Honey," and "Summoned by the Shadows." And yes, once again, I must mention the cover is a wonderful underwater vista, again by artist Yamada Akihiro, depicting a sort of grumpy looking Cthulhu -- perhaps grumpy because he's just been awakened from his aeons-old slumber! And his dark-eyed gaze seems to say to the viewer: buy this book -- or else!

While distant oases shimmer and hover high in the desert air, the Sentinels stand with little thought, and even less, nay, with no care for the Wanderers. Yet they brood and they stare in the still days and the dark nights. They brood and they stare as the desert storms arise as upflung oceans of sand, shredding flesh and tearing internal organs from the Wanderers' sand-scoured bones, drowning nomads' tents, and sundering the walls of citadels and towns in its mindless noise and fury. They brood and they stare in the proper seasons when ghouls and ghostly forms and shrieking sand-demons rise and rejoice upon their pedestal of finely scoured stone. For the Sentinels live, but not as terrestrial beings do. They remember how and when they came here from the utterly cold and remote reaches of space. They remember how the Old Ones came after them, and of the multitudes of races after them. But now, they sit there and wait, with a patience born out of eternity. Synopsis When avid model kit collector Danny discovers a " Pickman's Model " kit of a ferocious ghoul in a run-down antiques shop, he is delighted, and snaps up the bargain, immediately rushing home to build his new prize. Over the next couple of days, strange disappearances in his neighbourhood, along with subtle changes to the model which suggest it reacts in sympathy to the events, horrify Danny, and he attempts to destroy the artefact. --- Pickman's Muse.txt ---

[1] Ghoul L63
H. Vaughn. It was published in the Matthew Carpenter -edited anthology Pickman's Gallery by Ulthar Press in 2018. Synopsis The story charts the development of Richard Upton Pickman during his student days as a young artist railing against the stuffy, unchanging nature of the artistic community in the early 20th century, to the tempering of his work in order to gain acceptance by the local art patrons, and finally to realise what he needs to release his potential. At the same time it relates his relationships with two wildly different women, one the scion of a wealthy Boston family with a rebellious streak, the other a Ghoul working as entertainment in a disreputable speakeasy. Although both women provide him with inspiration for his work, in order to realise his true potential and become his muse, one must die at the hands of the other. Characters Richard Upton Pickman , a talented young artist who feels his work is directionless. Jane Channing , a young dilettante whose interest in Pickman leads to her gruesome demise. Althea , a stripper at a seedy nightclub, she uses a veil and strategically-placed feathers to hide her Ghoul nature.

--- Pnath [Abyss of Yhe.txt].txt ---

[1] Ghouls L79
P. Lovecraft Pnath is a region or city briefly mentioned as having been conquered by the city of Sarnath in " The Doom That Came to Sarnath " by H. P. Lovecraft . On the night of Sarnath's destruction, the king Nargis-Hei and his nobles were in the banquet hall of the royal palace, getting drunk on "ancient wine from the vaults of conquered Pnath". By the time of Randolph Carter 's visits to the Dreamlands, the vale of Pnath is a shunned area inhabited by the mysterious dholes . The floor is covered by half-eaten bones, as the Ghouls of the waking world use Pnath as a dumping ground to cast away "the refuse of their feastings", thrown from the edge of a crag that looms over the vale. Nodens night-gaunt servants "flop unendingly in the dark betwixt the Vale of Pnath and the passes to the outer world". Any intruders found on Mt. Ngranek are captured by the night-gaunts and taken to the vale of Pnath to be left to their own devices. ( HPL The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath

Into God-toys. The vegetation was sparse. Freakish grasses stabbed through the snow, denuded of color. --- Richard Upton Pickman.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L75
P. Lovecraft Richard Upton Pickman is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story " Pickman's Model ". He was a renowned Boston painter notorious for his graphic works. Biography Lovecraft's Work Pickman's origins are ambiguous. His artwork depicts the ghouls as having the habit of abducting human children and replacing them with "changelings": ghoul children that look deceptively human-like, left to be raised by humans. One of the children depicted bears an uncanny resemblance to Pickman himself, hinting that he might have been one of those changelings.

[2] Ghouls L81
One of the children depicted bears an uncanny resemblance to Pickman himself, hinting that he might have been one of those changelings. If true, this could explain his close association with ghouls ( HPL Pickman's Model "), and the fact that he apparently transformed into a ghoul himself at some point after his disappearance ( HPL The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath As an artist, Pickman had undeniable skill. " Boston never had a greater painter than Richard Upton Pickman," his one-time friend and devotee Thurber declared.

--- Rita Young.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L71
Growing up as part of a poor family in the American South, Rita is well acquainted with persecution, but as a strong independent young woman never let it get to her. Discovering from an early age that she possessed a natural ability as an athlete, Rita worked hard and managed to secure herself a track-and-field scholarship at Arkham 's prestigious Miskatonic University Ghouls of the Miskatonic Graham McNeill 's novel Ghouls of the Miskatonic expands on Rita's character considerably, showing that she has a certain knowledge of black magic, and perhaps even a degree of proficiency in its use. In the story, Rita and her best friend, roommate Amanda Sharpe , are kidnapped by a sinister cult of Cthulhu worshipers and their pet ghouls , but are eventually rescued by a ragtag group of people investigating the disappearances, including Rex Murphy and Finn Edwards Behind the Mythos The character of Rita Young was first introduced in the Arkham Horror Second Edition expansion Dunwich Horror .

--- Rogues in the House.txt ---

[2] Ghoul L627
Part-way down the stairs, he halted suddenly, his hair standing up. A vague bulk crouched in the darkness before him, a pair of eyes blazed like the eyes of a hunting beast. A beastlike snarl was the last thing he heard in life, as the monster lurched against him and a keen blade ripped through his belly. He gave one gasping cry and slumped down limply on the stairway. The barbarian loomed above him for an instant, ghoul-like, his eyes burning in the gloom. He knew the sound was heard, but the people in the Maze were careful to attend to their own business. A death cry on darkened stairs was nothing unusual. Later, some one would venture to investigate, but only after a reasonable lapse of time. Conan went up the stairs and halted at a door he knew well of old. It was fastened within, but his blade passed between the door and the jamb and lifted the bar.


--- Ross E. Lockhart.txt ---

[1] Ghoul L53
Lockhart Connection to the Mythos Author Editor Nationality United States Website Ross E. Lockhart is an American author and editor who has produced a number of works related to the Cthulhu Mythos begun with the writings of Howard Phillips Lovecraft . Working primarily in the fantasy, horror and supernatural genres, he has worked extensively in the small-press industry, and is the founder and editor-in-chief of Word Horde, a speciality publisher. --- Rough Night in Innsmouth.txt ---

[1] Ghoul L71
Luckily for the sailor, his friends come to his rescue, but this only serves to enrage the Mangler: sprouting huge claws from beneath his gloves, the by-now obviously inhuman creature goes berserk, attacking any and all in its way before the barman blows a small bone whistle, summoning a nine-foot-tall fish-like humanoid which kills the Mangler. The sailors make their escape in the subsequent panic, stealing the purse on their way out. Behind the Mythos The Boston Mangler is heavily implied to be a ghoul: the town from which he takes his title , the clawed hands and the description of looking " a little bit like "The Dog-Boy" [Max had] once seen in a carnival freak show " all point towards this conclusion. Similarly, the creature summoned by the bartender - who himself was said to have the Innsmouth Look - matches that of a Deep One A creature about nine feet in height ... It looked to be some hellish cross between fish and man ... It walked on two legs like a man, but had gills, bulging eyes and scaly skin like a fish.


--- Running the Night Whiskey.txt ---

[2] Ghouls L73
Leo brings his weapons. They walk into the trees, where there is a concealed cave. Donny lets out a wail, and something responds out of the darkness. Leo sees man-sized monsters with pale skin, broken teeth, and massive jaws come out of the cave. He prepares to shoot them, but Donny blocks the way, telling him that he will explain everything. Donny speaks of the war and the soldiers who died in the tunnels, trenches, and holes. There were whispers at night of dark creatures eating the corpses: ghouls. Donny says that he was called by the hungry dark, Umôrdhoth, and was saved by it in return of being fed. He opens the bottle of whiskey and pours it into the mouth of a ghoul. The ghoul begins to transform, its claws turning to talons, and spiked bones ripping through its flesh. Donny extends his hand to Leo, telling him that they don’t belong to this world anymore, but they will make a better one.

--- Sea Ghoul.txt ---

[1] Ghoul L1
НАЗВАНИЕ: Sea Ghoul ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:27:53 СИМВОЛОВ: 1007 Sea Ghoul Sociocultural Characteristics Origin The Bahamas Habitat Aquatic Real World Information First appearance EXP The Bermuda Triangle Created by Justin Schmid Sea Ghouls are a fictional aquatic variety of Ghouls that originate from the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game supplement The Bermuda Triangle Description As their name implies, Sea Ghouls are a marine variety of Ghouls which can be found in the seas around the Turks and Caicos Islands in the Bahamas, where they typically make their homes in sunken shipwrecks. Their diet consists mostly of fish, as well as the occasional lone swimmer. Unlike their land-based relatives, however, Sea Ghouls are cowardly creatures and thus never attack those who appear stronger than them, or who are part of a group. When they do attack, their strategy consists of savagely mauling their prey with their teeth and claws, while attempting to tear off oxygen tanks and other equipment, and holding down the victim until it drowns. ( EXP The Bermuda Triangle

--- Secret Santa.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L59
Getting in touch with one of his mysterious contacts to obtain both support and bait, Nathan then sets about preparing his ambush site, using magic to divine where the killer dubbed Evil Santa is to be found. Collecting the bait - a small girl named Amity - he sets her up in the exact spot the killer will be. When the man attempts to take the girl away, she stabs him with a bone shiv, and her family - a pack of vicious ghouls - emerge from below ground to spirit the body away and feed. Leaving just enough evidence for the police to make the connection between what remains at the murder site and Evil Santa, Nathan heads off to enjoy Christmas.


--- Secrets (Call of Cthulhu).txt ---

[1] Ghoul L89
Overview Vermont countryside? Investigators must uncover these secrets before they are destroyed by them. This Fright Night scenario pack is suitable for beginning keepers and investigators. The adventures can also be used by experienced keepers as interludes in a longer campaign. Included are numerous gray-scale illustrations, twenty authentic looking handouts, and a pair of maps. Back cover text The book contains four stand-alone scenarios designed to be plated over the course of a single session. All necessary handouts are included but, unusually, no pre-generated investigator characters. Closed Casket ": Robert Monroe-Tyler has just discovered that he is a ghoul , and fakes his own death to disappear and be with his people. When his casket is found to be filled with bricks, his distraught adoptive mother entreats the investigators to find out what became of him. A Love in Need ": the investigators stumble across a boarding house whose owners are killing their tenants in a ritual designed to save their disease-stricken son. The Unsealed Room ": when a bumbling occult investigator accidentally releases an imprisoned star vampire , its predations are mistaken by all involved for a vampire from folklore.

--- Shadows Dawning.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L63
She remembers how often the phone used to ring, with invites to dinner or simply to chat. But the police had helped spread the rumor that she was the primary suspect in John’s death, so her friends had stopped calling. Lita goes into John’s study, where she has set up a map with all of the information she had gathered about the cultists. The cultist she met gave her the name Ida Smith, and she finds an address for her in the telephone directory. Lita pours herself some scotch and lights a cigarette, thinking of her discovery of ghouls and the cultists that aided them. Early in the morning, Lita arrives in the outskirts on a bus. When she gets off, she notices a large number of abandoned houses, stores, and a church. Upon further investigation, Lita sees that the church door has brand new locks on it. She scouts the outside of the church, finding the back blocked by stacks of old wooden crates. Returning to the door, she sees strange symbols carved onto it, knowing she has found the cultists.

With her new apprentice, Pepper Kelly, Zorzi tracks the infamous Zanthu Tablets to Paris. But the city is rife with spies and the countess has many enemies. When Pepper is kidnapped, it becomes clear that someone is out for revenge. Zorzi must rescue her apprentice, find the tablets, and prevent an old enemy from summoning an army of vengeful ghouls from the depths of the catacombs. Stealing relics is a lot harder the second time around . . . --- Shuggob.txt ---

[1] Ghoul L23
НАЗВАНИЕ: Shuggob ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:29:02 СИМВОЛОВ: 1227 Shuggob Origin Vale of Pnath Dreamlands Occupation Sorcerer Species Ghoul First appearance EXP In the Vale of Pnath Created by Lin Carter Shuggob is a fictional character created by Lin Carter for his Cthulhu Mythos short story " In the Vale of Pnath Description Shuggob is an elderly ghoul sage who lives alone in a stone house surrounded by a garden of moss and lichens, with a hedge made of mottled fungi, in the part of the Dreamlands known as the Vale of Pnath . He is extremely knowledgeable about magic and skilled in the craft of potions. Somewhat unusually for a ghoul, Shuggob is a soft-spoken individual of gentlemanly demeanor and scholarly inclinations. He is amicable and receptive to strangers, offering them food and drinks of the type generally consumed by his species, i. e. made from human flesh and blood. In terms of physical appearance, Shuggob is tall and lean. His skin is grey, cold to the touch, and rubbery, and his hands are surprisingly strong.

--- Sinbad and the Great Old Ones.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L73
It was first published in April 2016 by Schlock! Publications; paperback, hardcover, and digital editions have all received a release. Synopsis When the Mad Arab Abdul Alhazred makes a bargain with Nyarlathotep to retrieve the four parts of the Sign of Koth and pave the way for the return of the Great Old Ones , legendary sailor Sinbad and a motley crew of heroic sidekicks are drawn into a race against time to stop the evil sorcerer. From the Indian Ocean to the Plateau of Leng , from Baghdad to Kadath , the group pursue their quarry across the known - and unknown - world, encountering such diverse threats as feral ghouls , flying Shantak-birds , predatory Spiders of Leng , ravenous Tcho-Tchos , and marauding Star Spawn . Although successful in his quest, virtually all of his companions and the entirety of his crew meet a grizzly death at the hands of one monstrous being or another.

--- So Runs the World Away.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L69
Kiernan Country United States Language English Portuguese Publisher Robinson Publication The Mammoth Book of Vampire Stories by Women Publication date October 2001 "So Runs the World Away" is a short story by American author Caitlin R. Kiernan that introduces her setting of the supernatural underworld of Providence Rhode Island , which she used as the milieu for several subsequent stories. It was first published in 2001 in The Mammoth Book of Vampire Stories by Women . It was later reprinted in Kiernan's collection To Charles Fort, With Love , and in their 2018 Cthulhu Mythos omnibus Houses Under the Sea Overview The story focuses on an undead creature known as Dead Girl who seems to have trouble fitting in to the societies of ghouls and vampires who dominate the Providence dark world. She is preoccupied with remembering the human life she had before her transition, an impulse discouraged by the character known as The Bailiff: "We forget for a reason, child," he tells her. "Time is too heavy to carry so much of it strung about our necks." The story introduces characters and settings that will play important roles in later fiction by Kiernan, including The Bailiff, Madame Terpsichore, and the house on Benefit Street.

[2] Ghoul L77
She is preoccupied with remembering the human life she had before her transition, an impulse discouraged by the character known as The Bailiff: "We forget for a reason, child," he tells her. "Time is too heavy to carry so much of it strung about our necks." It begins to sketch out Kiernan's vision of ghoul society, elaborated from the hints in H. P. Lovecraft 's " Pickman's Model Locations The "big", "yellow" house on Benefit Street, described as "a house filled up with things that are pretty or broken or both." The aboveground portion of the house is occupied by vampires, described as "stiff and obsolescent beings... tragic waxwork shades sipping absinthe"; the basement is an entrance to the subterranean warrens of the ghouls.

[3] Ghouls L87
It begins to sketch out Kiernan's vision of ghoul society, elaborated from the hints in H. P. Lovecraft 's " Pickman's Model Locations The "big", "yellow" house on Benefit Street, described as "a house filled up with things that are pretty or broken or both." The aboveground portion of the house is occupied by vampires, described as "stiff and obsolescent beings... tragic waxwork shades sipping absinthe"; the basement is an entrance to the subterranean warrens of the ghouls. In Kiernan's 2007 novel Daughter of Hounds , its address is given as 135 Benefit Street--explicitly identifying it with the house that served as the model for the Lovecraft story " The Shunned House The bottom of Providence's Sekonk River is where Dead Girl, Bobby, and Gable sleep during the day--the latter "coiled like an eel in the roots of a drowned willow". The Swan Point Cemetery has a mausoleum for the Stanton family where Dead Girl keeps a cigar box full of secrets.

[4] Ghouls L107
The story also contains a description of Lovecraft's gravesite in the cemetery, as well as a nearby tree where fans have carved the "unpronounceable names of dark, fictitious gods and entire passages from Lovecraft," as well "a scar in the shape of a tentacle-headed fish, a parody of the Christian ichthus." Characters Dead Girl , an undead woman who sleeps at the bottom of the Sekonk River. It's unclear whether she is a vampire or something else; she is acquainted with both vampires and ghouls but does not seem to be part of either society. She has memories, possibly stolen, of being a living human in the modern era, taking a boyfriend to see Lovecraft's grave, but she also has an attachment to a newspaper article about a suspected 19th century vampire named Mercy Lena Brown. (Brown was a real person who was actually accused of vampirism after her death.) Bobby , Dead Girl's companion. He is described as having "quicksilver eyes", which in Kiernan's fiction generally indicates vampirism.

[1] Ghouls L51
НАЗВАНИЕ: Spawn of Nyogtha ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:29:14 СИМВОЛОВ: 1158 Spawn of Nyogtha Sociocultural Characteristics Also known as Blasphemous Children of the Dark Origin Nyogtha Real World Information First appearance EXP Ye Booke of Monstres II Created by Scott David Aniolowski The Spawn of Nyogtha are a fictional race created in 1995 by Chaosium for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game. Background The Spawn of Nyogtha are produced by the blasphemous unions between ghouls , humans, and Nyogtha . Within three-to-six decades, they degenerate into shapeless abominations. During the first decades they easily pass for a human. Running through their bodies is not blood but a viscous black ichor. They are charismatic, strong, and tough creatures whom serve Nyogtha and seduce others into its cult. Once degeneration begins, within a few months they complete their metamorphosis. Which starts with hideous black splotches appearing on the flesh which quickly spread, while the spawn becomes ravenous.

--- Stories_0923bad7d6 [Clark Ashton Smith, The Nameless Offspring.txt].txt ---

[1] Ghoul L693
Certain evasive, incoherent hints appeared to point themselves suddenly to an atrocious and abhorrent whole. With imperfect success, I assured myself that the thing I had fancied was incredible to science; was a mere creation of superstitious diablerie. No, it could not be . . . here in England, of all places . . . that corpse-devouring demon of Oriental tales and legends, . . . the ghoul. Contrary to my fears, there was no repetition of the fiendish howling as we passed the secret room. But I thought that I heard a measured crunching, such as a large animal would make in devouring its food. My room, though still drear and dismal enough, had been cleared of its accumulated dust and matted gossamers. After a personal inspection, Sir John left me and retired to his own chamber.

--- Stories_b3b29928d7 [Robert Bloch, The Shambler from the Stars.txt].txt ---

[1] Ghouls L133
But not for long. Ambition, ever an illusion, was the cause of my undoing. I wanted to write a real story; not the stereotyped, ephemeral sort of tale I turned out for the magazines, but a real work of art. The creation of such a masterpiece became my ideal. I was not a good writer, but that was not entirely due to my errors in mechanical style. It was, I felt, the fault of my subject matter. Vampires, werewolves, ghouls, mythological monsters—these things constituted material of little merit. Commonplace imagery, ordinary adjectival treatment, and a prosaically anthropocentric point of view were the chief detriments to the production of a really good weird tale. I must have new subject matter, truly unusual plot material. If only I could conceive of something that was teratologically incredible! I longed to learn the songs the demons sing as they swoop between the stars, or hear the voices of the olden gods as they whisper their secrets to the echoing void.

Although the effects of the nepenthe preserved the body of the Outsider beyond all known substances, the damp conditions of the cavern slowly began to affect the dead flesh of the Outsider. Had he been buried in Egypt with its dry and hot climate, the nepenthe would have preserved the Outsider's body for a thousand years before the first signs of decay would have begun to form.

[7] Ghoul L265
However, in just two hundred years in the castle-tomb, the flesh of the Outsider began to show early stages of decomposition. While the body of the Outsider wondered mindlessly though the dark castle, in the outside cavern a forest had grown where one lone tree had struggled to survive eighty years earlier. Natural selection had provided the vaulted cave with a most amazing underground forest, unlike any place else on earth. For the next seventy five years the Outsider was a lone ghoul within the castle-tomb, but in the two-hundred and fifty-fifth year after sipping the black elixir of eternity, the next amazing event took place: the Outsider began to dream. Although he remained a soulless being without memories, some sort of mind began to develop and emerge, the result -- possibly -- of the ka interacting with a physical body. The first form of activity that this new mind began to exhibit was an imageless dream, even as the body continued to wander the halls of the castle-tomb.

--- The Creeper in the Crypt.txt ---

[2] Ghouls L91
" Dark also claimed that the tenants of the graveyard "would come to visit the house from below when a wizard invoked it with the proper spells and sacrifice." The Graveyard on the Hill Next to the Chambers house is "the old graveyard on the hill"; this corresponds to the "Wooded Graveyard" on "Hangman's Hill" that appears on Lovecraft's map. Dark claimed that below the graveyard there were "tunnels and burrows and secret vaults used in witch-days for unhallowed rites", and that these vaults had "tenants". Bloch does not specify who these tenants are, but it's clear that they are meant to be ghouls, like those that appear in Lovecraft's " Pickman's Model ": bestial, anthropophagic, subterranean creatures who often dwell beneath cemeteries. The story includes a few other Arkham landmarks, most mentioned in passing--like the Carter house, a possible reference to the house in Lovecraft's " The Unnamable In 1818, the new government intervened to "destroy some particularly atrocious burrows in and about some of the more ancient houses and, incidentally, to dig up a graveyard better left untouched." (The "new" government is presumably federal, since the current Massachusetts government traces back to 1629; in 1818, the U. S. president was James Monroe.

Whenever the Star Spawn appeared, the Dreamless went mad at the sight and both Deathless and Ophidians fell to their might. Tsan Chan was saved from annihilation by two things. Some grew at incredible rates and some could follow orders.

It was first published in Weird Tales in January 1935. Synopsis Namirrha, an arrogant sorcerer, is destroyed by his own hubris. He makes war on the Emperor Zotulla and his Empire of Xylac. Ten Original Dark Tales Publication date "The Dead and the Moonstruck" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that first appeared in the 2004 collection Gothic! Ten Original Dark Tales . Set like several of Kiernan's stories in the supernatural underworld of Providence Rhode Island , "The Dead and the Moonstruck" tells the tale of a changeling--a human child raised by ghouls --facing a coming-of-age ordeal. Behind the Mythos The title comes from a passage from H. P. Lovecraft Supernatural Horror in Literature Children will always be afraid of the dark, and men with minds sensitive to hereditary impulse will always tremble at the thought of the hidden and fathomless worlds of strange life which may pulsate in the gulfs beyond the stars, or press hideously upon our own globe in unholy dimensions which only the dead and the moonstruck can glimpse.

--- The Doom of Yakthoob.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L59
It is the first of a series of short fiction pieces Carter offered as autobiographical sketches by Abdul Alhazred from the Necronomicon The story concerns Alhazred's education, in which he "learned the summoning-up of Evil Things." It introduced Yakthoob, the "notorious Saracen wizard" who served as Alhazred's mentor, as well as "the languid and dissolute Ibn Ghazoul," Alhazred's fellow student and closest friend. The plot explains how Yakthoob met a gruesome end due to Ibn Ghazoul's selfish indulgence of vices. Carter describes Alhazred's initiation into esoteric knowledge as taking place in Egypt : He "conversed with ghouls in the rock tombs of Neb and even partook of the unnamed Feasts of Nitocris in loathsome crypts beneath the Great Pyramid," descended the Secret Stairs to the "black catacombs below the crumbling ruins of elder and ghoulhaunted Memphis," and performed "Blasphemous Rites" In the "noxious caverns of Nephren-Ka in the sealed and unknown Valley of Hadoth by the Nile." After its initial appearance in The Arkham Collector (including the hardbound omnibus The Arkham Collector: Volume I ), "The Doom of Yakthoob" was reprinted in the Yuletide 1985 issue of Crypt of Cthulhu (#36), and again in the Candlemas 1990 issue (#70). It was included in the Cthulhu Mythos anthologies The New Lovecraft Circle Fedogan & Bremer , 1996) and The Necronomicon: Selected Stories and Essays Concerning the Blasphemous Tome of the Mad Arab Chaosium , 1996).


--- The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L209
Carter boards a ship sailing to Baharna , a great seaport on the isle of Oriab. On the way to Oriab and while he travels across the island riding a zebra, Carter hears dark whispers about the night-gaunts , though they are never properly described. Carter makes a treacherous climb across Ngranek and discovers the gigantic carving of the gods on its far side. He is surprised to see that the features match those of sailors who trade at the port of Celephaïs , but before he can act on this knowledge, he is snatched away by the night-gaunts and left to die in the Vale of Pnath in the underworld Carter is rescued by friendly ghouls , amongst them Richard Pickman , a friend of Carter's, the protagonist of another of Lovecraft's stories, " Pickman's Model " and who is now also a ghoul, who agree to return him to the upper Dreamlands. They make their way to the terrible city of the gugs to reach the Tower of Koth, wherein a winding stairway leads to the surface. Finding the city asleep, Carter and the ghouls attempt to sneak past the snoring gugs. The ghasts , the gugs' traditional enemies, begin an attack, but the group manages to ascend the stairway and open the great trapdoor to the Enchanted Wood.

[8] Ghoul L455
( HPL Selected Letters II) In 1948, Arthur C. Clarke sent Lord Dunsany a copy of The Arkham Sampler containing part of The Dream-Quest . Dunsany responded: "I see Lovecraft borrowed my style, & I don't grudge it to him". Connections to other Lovecraft tales The ghoul Richard Upton Pickman first appeared in " Pickman's Model " (1927) in which he is still human and painting nightmare creatures he calls forth as models. The priest Atal appears as a boy and youth in two earlier tales, " The Cats of Ulthar " (1920) and " The Other Gods " (1933), respectively, which fully describe events alluded to in The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath Nyarlathotep , the Crawling Chaos, is frequently mentioned in Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos tales, but his appearance here is the only time he interacts meaningfully with any of Lovecraft's characters.

[9] Ghouls L583
Kadath is also briefly mentioned in At the Mountains of Madness The Sign of Koth is mentioned in The Case of Charles Dexter Ward as inscribed on a tower in the dreamworld (to keep the gugs from returning to upper dreamland) and as having strange attributes. It is also inscribed in the catacombs under Curwen 's long abandoned house. Neither novelette was published in Lovecraft's lifetime. --- The Dwellers Under the Tombs.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L99
As they were forced lower into the hills, they retreated along the evolutionary scale as well--until they were, as Conrad exclaims after he encounters them: "Crawling obscenities seething in the slime of the earth’s unguessed deeps—the ultimate horror of retrogression—the nadir of human degeneration—good God, their ancestors were men!" One thing that distinguishes these creatures from their European counterparts is that their heads resemble those of dogs rather than snakes--one is called "a flaming-eyed dog-headed horror such as madmen see in black nightmares"--perhaps influenced by H. P. Lovecraft ghouls . The Dagoth Hills creatures do, however, share with Howard's European throwbacks "an earthy, reptilian sort of smell."

[1] Ghoul L155
He returns just in time to hear Mayhew reciting the summoning, and sees the Fishers from Outside descend from the skies and tear the Professor apart, to the point that the body is only identifiable by his pince-nez glasses. Behind the Mythos "The Fishers from Outside" features a tip of the hat to "Winged Death" by having a main character named Sloan, and mentioning a posthumous character named Slauenwite. In "Winged Death", the main character is named Slauenwite, and a posthumous character named Sloane is mentioned. The name "Yogash" for the manservant of the ship captain Abner Hoag is identical to that of Yogash the Black ( HPL The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath ) and Yogash the Ghoul HPL Selected Letters 4.617). However, since Hoag's manservant is described as a human / Deep One hybrid, he might not be the same character as Yogash the Ghoul.

НАЗВАНИЕ: The Ghoul ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:31:19 СИМВОЛОВ: 1666 The Ghoul Author Clark Ashton Smith Country United States Language English Genre(s) Fantasy, Horror Publication The Fantasy Fan Publication date January 1934 The Ghoul " is a short fantasy-horror story by Clark Ashton Smith , published in January 1934 in the amateur publication The Fantasy Fan . It tells the tale of Noureddin Hassan, who is accused of murdering seven people to fulfill a ghoul's demand to protect his wife's grave. The story explores themes of grief, horror, and moral conflict. Synopsis "The Ghoul" follows the story of Noureddin Hassan, a respected man from Bussorah. After the death of his beloved wife, Amina, he is consumed by grief.

[2] Ghoul L49
It tells the tale of Noureddin Hassan, who is accused of murdering seven people to fulfill a ghoul's demand to protect his wife's grave. The story explores themes of grief, horror, and moral conflict. Synopsis "The Ghoul" follows the story of Noureddin Hassan, a respected man from Bussorah. After the death of his beloved wife, Amina, he is consumed by grief. Mourning at her grave, he encounters a ghoul who demands a horrifying bargain: Noureddin must bring the ghoul a body each night for eight nights, specifically those he has killed himself, to spare Amina's grave from desecration.

Synopsis "The Ghoul" follows the story of Noureddin Hassan, a respected man from Bussorah. After the death of his beloved wife, Amina, he is consumed by grief. Mourning at her grave, he encounters a ghoul who demands a horrifying bargain: Noureddin must bring the ghoul a body each night for eight nights, specifically those he has killed himself, to spare Amina's grave from desecration. Although poetically described as a demon the creature in this story is clearly intended to be a classical Ghoul of Arabia Behind the Mythos The 1933 movie The Ghoul starring Boris Karloff was an Egypt -based story about a vengeful mummy , however the redolent influence of that popular piece of cinema should not be ignored. (relevance or source Smith saw the film?) The more proximate influence for this story is without question the body of Arab folklore compiled in the Arabian Nights , specifically by way of William Beckford's novel Vathek (1786).

[5] Ghoul L85
(relevance or source Smith saw the film?) The more proximate influence for this story is without question the body of Arab folklore compiled in the Arabian Nights , specifically by way of William Beckford's novel Vathek (1786). The historical figure on whom Beckford based Vathek is the Caliph Al-Wathiq (full name Abu Jaffar Harun al-Wathiq ibn Mutasim), who was born in AD 816, and reigned from AD 842 to 847, which sets "The Ghoul" in the mid-840's.

--- The Ghulistan Affair.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L49
Synopsis The story is for the most part a conversation between two men, implied to be special agents in the employ of the British government, on the state of affairs regarding the various non-human humanoid creatures which inhabit a vague geographical region incorporating India to Central Asia. In particular, their discourse revolves around an ill-fated expedition to an area known as the Land of Ghouls , and their ultimate realisation that one of the few survivors was, most likely, a ghoul himself. The story concludes with what appears to be noises of an attack on their safe house, and the implication that ghoul footsoldiers have come to wipe out all those who know of their existence. Behind the Mythos One of the names mentioned by the men in connection with their topic is Swami Chandraputra , although both confess to having been an able to find anyone with knowledge on who that may be.


--- The Graveyard Rats.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L93
Aware of the rat problem, he wages a covert war with the beasts for years, as they keep dragging off the bodies which he is intent on looting. When one night Masson unearths a body just as the creatures are dragging it off, he crawls down the oversized tunnel in an attempt to retrieve it. However, he is ambushed by the rats in the warren, and then attacked by an animated corpse before becoming trapped in a dead-end tunnel and suffocating. Connections While the story has no explicit references to Mythos elements, its depiction of corpse-eating humanoids who tunnel below cemeteries, a "moribund, inhuman life that was said to exist in forgotten burrows in the earth," seems to owe a great deal to Lovecraft's ghouls , as they appeared in stories like " Pickman's Model Kuttner's suggestion of "blasphemous secrets and mysteries... said to be hidden in subterranean cellars and caverns, where forgotten pagan rites were still celebrated in defiance of law and sanity" by "evil cults that worshipped Hecate and the dark Magna Mater in frightful orgies" evokes stories like " The Rats in the Walls " and " The Horror at Red Hook The setting of "ancient, witch-haunted Salem," whose "dark gabled houses still leaned perilously towards each other over narrow cobbled streets," strongly recalls Lovecraft's Arkham Characters Old Masson, a graverobbing cemetery caretaker.

[1] Ghoul L1
НАЗВАНИЕ: The Grinning Ghoul ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:31:23 СИМВОЛОВ: 2400 The Grinning Ghoul Author Robert Bloch Language English Genre(s) Cthulhu Mythos Publication Weird Tales Publication date June 1936 WT "The Grinning Ghoul" is a short story by Robert Bloch that first appeared in the June 1936 issue of Weird Tales . The plot, involving a psychiatrist whose attempts to treat a patient put the doctor himself in a sanitarium, reflects the fact that Bloch was "long skeptical of the pretensions of psychiatrists... regarding them as little more than shamans in suits." Synopsis The narrator is an "inmate of a sanitorium for mental cases" who six months earlier was a "well-known and moderately successful practicing psychiatrist".

[2] Ghouls L53
The plot, involving a psychiatrist whose attempts to treat a patient put the doctor himself in a sanitarium, reflects the fact that Bloch was "long skeptical of the pretensions of psychiatrists... regarding them as little more than shamans in suits." Synopsis The narrator is an "inmate of a sanitorium for mental cases" who six months earlier was a "well-known and moderately successful practicing psychiatrist". In an effort to treat Alexander Chaupin, a professor at Newberry College, who has recurring nightmares about ghouls living beneath Misericorde Cemetery, the doctor insists that the two of them visit the graveyard at night to demonstrate that the creatures he fears are imaginary. When Chaupin leads the doctor to a tomb, he is surprised to find that there is indeed a secret opening there--giving access to stairways that drop deep into the earth. At the bottom is a vast cavern system, where Chaupin leaves the doctor, saying he will bring back proof that his stories are true. Instead, the doctor hears a cry, then "the rustling scrape of frantic movement", then a "hoarse barking", a "bestial growling" that sickens him with "its semi-human tones".

[3] Ghouls L55
When Chaupin leads the doctor to a tomb, he is surprised to find that there is indeed a secret opening there--giving access to stairways that drop deep into the earth. At the bottom is a vast cavern system, where Chaupin leaves the doctor, saying he will bring back proof that his stories are true. Instead, the doctor hears a cry, then "the rustling scrape of frantic movement", then a "hoarse barking", a "bestial growling" that sickens him with "its semi-human tones". The doctor races up the stairs, and slams the secret portal shut in the face of the pursuing ghouls--but not before he sees that the leader of the pack is Professor Chaupin. Behind the Mythos In an effort to convince the doctor of the truth of his claims, Chaupin cites a number of Cthulhu Mythos tomes: " Ludvig Prinn Mysteries of the Worm ", "the grotesque Black Rites of mystic Luveh-Keraphf , the priest of cryptic Bast ", and "the mad and legendary Necronomicon of Abdul Alhazred ".

--- The Hound (short story).txt ---

[1] Ghoul L143
The collection consists of headstones, preserved bodies, skulls and several heads in different phases of decomposition. It also included statues, frightful paintings and a locked portfolio, bound in tanned human skin. One day, they learn of a particular grave, which sparks a profound interest in them, an old grave in a Holland cemetery, which holds a legendary tomb raider within. One who was said to have stolen, many years ago, a "potent thing from an mighty sepulcher". One night, they travel to this old cemetery where the ancient "ghoul" was buried. The thought of exhuming the final resting place of a former grave robber is irresistibly appealing to them. That, and the fact that the body had been buried several centuries before, drives them to travel such long distances to reach the site. Upon reaching the old cemetery, they notice the distant baying of a giant hound. They ignore it and begin their excavation. After a while of digging they hit a solid object in the ground.

[2] Ghoul L147
They ignore it and begin their excavation. After a while of digging they hit a solid object in the ground. They clear the last of the dirt from it and happen upon a strange and elaborately made coffin. Upon opening the casket, they are surprised to find that after several centuries the remains are still intact. Several places, on the skeletal remains, seem torn and shattered, as if attacked by a wild animal. Yet the whole of the skeleton is still completely distinguishable. At that moment, they notice a jade amulet hanging from the "ghoul's" neck. They examine it and after a bit of observation they recognize the amulet as one mentioned in "the forbidden Necronomicon of the mad Arab Abdul Alhazred". They immediately know they must have the amulet at all cost. They remove it from the skeleton and flee to their homes. As they do, they notice once again the continuous sound of a hound 's baying in the distance. Even as they return home, strange sounds can be heard in their house, including the distant sound of the hound.

[3] Ghoul L209
All too well did we trace the sinister lineaments described by the old Arab daemonologist; lineaments, he wrote, drawn from some obscure supernatural manifestation of the souls of those who vexed and gnawed at the dead. The reference to "Leng" is one of the first mentions of Lovecraft's imaginary plateau, having only appeared before in 1920s " Celephaïs ". Here placed in Central Asia, Leng is also associated in Lovecraft's writings with Antarctica and his imaginary Dreamlands Lovecraftian scholar Will Murray , pointing to the "semi-canine face" on the amulet as well as the "corpse-eating cult" of Leng, suggests that the titular creature of "The Hound" "probably represents an early form of the ghoul as Lovecraft would develop it." Folklore This story has certain parallels to the folkloric tradition of the church grim, a spectral entity that takes the form of a large black dog and serves as a guardian spirit of churchyards. The church grim protects the consecrated ground of a churchyard by attacking those who would desecrate it through grave robbery and vandalism. Adaptations In 1972, Jack Jackson adapted the story for the indie anthology comic Skull by Last Gasp Eco-Funnies.

--- The New Annotated H. P. Lovecraft.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L69
Klinger reanimates Lovecraft with clarity and historical insight, charting the rise of the erstwhile pulp writer, whose rediscovery and reclamation into the literary canon can be compared only to that of Poe or Melville. Weaving together a broad base of existing scholarship with his own original insights, Klinger appends Lovecraft's uncanny oeuvre and Kafkaesque life story in a way that provides context and unlocks many of the secrets of his often cryptic body of work. Over the course of his career, Lovecraft―"the Copernicus of the horror story" ( Fritz Leiber )―made a marked departure from the gothic style of his predecessors that focused mostly on ghosts, ghouls, and witches, instead crafting a vast mythos in which humanity is but a blissfully unaware speck in a cosmos shared by vast and ancient alien beings. One of the progenitors of "weird fiction," Lovecraft wrote stories suggesting that we share not just our reality but our planet, and even a common ancestry, with unspeakable, godlike creatures just one accidental revelation away from emerging from their epoch of hibernation and extinguishing both our individual sanity and entire civilization. --- The Night Ocean.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L61
P. Lovecraft is a short story first published in The Californian vol. 4, no. 3 (Winter 1936). Possibly able to be considered a prose poem rather than a conventional short story, this very short tale is about a man who spends most of a year at a small coastal town. A series of deaths occurs, disappearances of swimmers including those strong and skilled enough for such deaths to be most unlikely. During a mighty storm the unnamed narrator see humanoid but inhuman figures emerging on the deserted beach. After the storm, when the beach has been cleansed by the waves, he finds a decaying human hand and realises that the sea creatures, ghosts, sea ghouls or whatever they may be- are indeed destroying swimmers. With a progressive melancholy the narrator watches the seasons pass until on the night of a preternatural full moon he sees the strange figures emerge again and is unsure if they are dogs, humans or diseased fish- but they are inhuman.

--- The Outsider.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L161
God knows it was not of this world — or no longer of this world — yet to my horror I saw in its eaten-away and bone-revealing outlines a leering, abhorrent travesty of the human shape; and in its mouldy, disintegrating apparel an unspeakable quality that chilled me even more. In his shock and surprise, he loses his balance and touches the creature. Horrified, he runs from the building back to his castle, where he tries unsuccessfully to crawl back through the grate into his old world. Cast out of his old existence, the narrator now rides with the "mocking and friendly ghouls on the night wind," forever and officially an outsider since the moment he stretched his fingers towards the creature in the darkness and felt nothing but the "cold and unyielding surface of polished glass," signifying he had touched a mirror. Prior to telling of how he discovered that the monster was, in fact, himself, the narrator explains that he fled to a valley of the Nile in Egypt, where he exists alongside other outsiders - presumably undead, like himself - and even enjoys something of a social life (for example, a feast beneath one of the Pyramids), although he describes how " nepenthe has calmed me", hinting that he is still trying to forget his haunted past.

[2] Ghouls L207
The idea of "becoming other" parallels what is happening in this story. The intensity of the process is heightened because the reader is learning of this transition from the human to the abhuman right along with the narrator, who is learning it himself. Synopsis At the pre-opening meeting for an art exhibition celebrating the works and legacy of the enigmatic Richard Upton Pickman , a mismatched group of organisers, artists and journalists decide to take a trip to see the supposed studio of their hero, which one believes to have located beneath an abandoned Boston warehouse. Upon reaching the warehouse and breaking in, the group do manage to locate the studio, but are quickly set upon by a pack of ghouls which boil up from the well located in the basement's centre. Only two of the group survive the attack and make a successful escape. Behind the Mythos "The Pickman Revival" features several nods to the Cthulhu Mythos in addition to the Pickman paintings on display. These include the location of the exhibition, Innsmouth ; one of the artists having subtle signs of the Innsmouth Look , as well as painting pictures of fish-men hybrids and enormous creatures with cephalopod traits ; and another who admits to being a ghoul himself.

--- The Rats in the Walls.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L117
( HPL commonplace book 79) Steven J. Mariconda points to Sabine Baring-Gould's Curious Myths of the Middle Ages (1862—68) as a source for Lovecraft's story. The description of the cavern under the priory has many similarities to Baring-Gould's account of St. Patrick's Purgatory, a legendary Irish holy site, and the story of the priory's rats sweeping across the landscape may have been inspired by the book's retelling of the legend of Bishop Hatto, who was devoured by rats after he set fire to starving peasants during a famine. ( EXP : "Baring-Gould and the Ghouls", The Horror of It All ) See the story of the Mouse Tower of Bingen. Parts of Lovecraft's story bear a striking resemblance to Carl Jung's famous "house" dream (told to Sigmund Freud in 1909, though not well known before 1925): the descent through one's historically-stratified ancestral family home to a Romanesque cellar; lifting a hidden slab; descending stone steps to a prehistoric cave littered with bones, broken pottery, etc.

Behind the Mythos Written by Dan O'Bannon , the plot of the film borrows from the Lovecraft original, and follows some of the concepts in the original story. --- The Stairs in the Crypt.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L59
Synopsis When the necromancer Avalzaunt dies, in ancient Hyperborea , his body is "preserved in a bath of bituminous natron" by his disciples, as per the deceased's own instructions, and interred in a crypt that he himself had designed. The eldest disciple, Mygon, inherits the tower in which his master lived. A few years pass while Avalzaunt's mummified body gathers enough strength to revive itself. When he does so, he opens up a passage to the stairs that lead to the underground lairs of the canine Ghouls . In life, Avalzaunt was a friend of the Ghouls and a worshiper of their deity, Nyogtha , so when they finally enter the chamber, he asks them for some blood to drink. Offered a beverage made from a rotten corpse's fluids, the revived sorcerer finds that it does nothing to quench his thirst. Instead, he realises that he needs fresh warm human blood, straight from the veins of the living. Avalzaunt and his Ghoul pack kill each of the sorcerer's former acolytes, starting with Mygon, and drink all their blood.

--- The Studies of Dr. Reid.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L65
Reid Author Peter Rawlik Language English Publisher Ulthar Press Publication Pickman's Gallery Publication date The Studies of Dr. Reid " is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Peter Rawlik . It was published in the thematic anthology Pickman's Gallery by Ulthar Press in 2018. Synopsis Dr. Reid explains to Eliot, the silent "audience" from " Pickman's Model ", how he had observed the artist Richard Upton Pickman for a time before his disappearance, noticing several unusual characteristics which he had been developing over time. Reid had later followed Pickman on his nightly jaunts, and watched his trysts with the ghouls which became the subject of his art. Fascinated, Reid began to study taxidermy in an effort to understand the biology of the creatures, and eventually worked up the courage to kill one, later dissecting it. The story ends with the revelation that Reid has brought Eliot to a subterranean nest of ghouls, where he wants the poor man to aid him in procuring another sample for the dissection table. Characters Dr. Reid , a learned man with an unhealthy interest in the creatures which prowl the Boston streets at night.

НАЗВАНИЕ: The Thousand-and-Third Tale of Scheherazade ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:33:22 СИМВОЛОВ: 2144 The Thousand-and-Third Tale of Scheherazade Author Caitlin R. Kiernan Language English Publication Sirenia Digest Publication date January 2009 "The Thousand-and-Third Tale of Scheherazade" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan set in the milieu of the ghouls of Providence . It first appeared in the January 2009 issue of Sirenia Digest (#38), and was later reprinted in Kiernan's collection Confessions of a Five-Chambered Heart (Subterranean Press, 2012). The story is set in "the terrible old house on Federal Hill," a place used by the changelings, humans kidnapped as infants and raised to serve as servants of the ghouls: For more than two centuries now, this place has served as a refuge for the Children of the Cuckoo, those stolen as infants and raised up in the warrens below College Hill to labor and officiate for the Hounds of Cain, to walk abroad in the day-lit world where the ghouls dare not venture. It introduces a third class besides the ghouls and changelings: humans kidnapped as adults and treated as slaves by ghoul and changeling alike--described as "the men and women kept downstairs, inside the filthy cages built into the sub-basement of the old house." The story describes the relationship between a changeling, a female assassin, and a male slave who "was a scholar, once."

[3] Ghouls L55

The story also mentions the Bailiff, a character who plays a prominent part in Daughter of Hounds and appears in several other Kiernan stories.

--- The Warm.txt ---

[1] Ghoul L67
НАЗВАНИЕ: The Warm ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:33:35 СИМВОЛОВ: 1493 The Warm Author Darrell Schweitzer Language English Genre(s) Cthulhu Mythos Publisher Titan Books Publication The Madness of Cthulhu: Volume 1 Publication date October 2014 The Warm " is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Darrell Schweitzer . It was first published in the S. T. Joshi -edited anthology The Madness of Cthulhu: Volume 1 in October 2014. Synopsis "The Warm" is a retelling of H. P. Lovecraft 's 1927 short story " Pickman's Model " but told from the perspective of the ghoul , itself something of an outcast from its own society, who first inspired Richard Upton Pickman 's most controversial works. Pickman befriends the creature, persuading it to pose for him, then later encouraging it to tell him stories of its kin to be used as subject matter. However, through extended contact, the ghoul begins to become more human as Pickman becomes more animalistic. Although the creature wants the man to introduce it to human society he refuses and, in despair, the ghoul summons its fellows who take Pickman below ground to join them, as shown in the finale of "Pickman's Model".

[2] Ghoul L75
T. Joshi -edited anthology The Madness of Cthulhu: Volume 1 in October 2014. Synopsis "The Warm" is a retelling of H. P. Lovecraft 's 1927 short story " Pickman's Model " but told from the perspective of the ghoul , itself something of an outcast from its own society, who first inspired Richard Upton Pickman 's most controversial works. НАЗВАНИЕ: The White Elephant ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:33:38 СИМВОЛОВ: 623 The White Elephant Full story online here Author H. P. Lovecraft R. H. Barlow Country USA Language English Publication The Fantastic Poetry Date of writing Publication date "The White Elephant" is a poem written by H. P. Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow on 23 May 1934. It was published for the first time in the 1990 Lovecraft collection The Fantastic Poetry Synopsis The poem describes a mysterious man or entity who rose from "primal chaos" and commanded "lesser ghouls " to perform rites for him. They bred poisonous flowers and trees, and created a "white beast" made from "fungous dust", which pagans now pray to.

--- The_Dream-Quest_of_Unknown_Kadath_The_H.P._Lovecraft_Wiki_Fandom_8d0c07186d.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L305
Carter makes a treacherous climb across Ngranek and discovers the gigantic carving of the gods on its far side. He is surprised to see that the features match those of sailors who trade at the port of Celephaïs, but before he can act on this knowledge, he is snatched away by the night-gaunts and left to die in the Vale of Pnath in the underworld. Carter is rescued by friendly ghouls, amongst them Richard Pickman, a friend of Carter's, the protagonist of another of Lovecraft's stories, "Pickman's Model" and who is now also a ghoul, who agree to return him to the upper Dreamlands. They make their way to the terrible city of the gugs to reach the Tower of Koth, wherein a winding stairway leads to the surface. Finding the city asleep, Carter and the ghouls attempt to sneak past the snoring gugs. The ghasts, the gugs' traditional enemies, begin an attack, but the group manages to ascend the stairway and open the great trapdoor to the Enchanted Wood.

[4] Ghouls L329
When the slant-eyed man is momentarily distracted, Carter pushes him into the well and escapes through the maze-like corridors. In pitch-black darkness, Carter wanders through the monastery, fearing he is being pursued by the High Priest Not to Be Described. At last reaching the outside, Carter realizes that he is in the ruins of ancient Sarkomand, which lies near the coast. Soon he encounters the ghouls that helped him earlier once more. The Men of Leng have taken them hostage on their ship, and they are to be taken to the nameless rock, revealed to be a moon-beast outpost. Carter summons the rest of the ghouls from the underworld and they take control of the galley. After releasing their kin, they sail on to the nameless rock and fight a pitched battle against the moon-beasts.

Finally a great procession arrives with much fanfare, led by a pharaoh-like man who explains to Carter that the gods of earth have seen the city of Carter's dreams and decided to make it their home, and have thus abandoned Kadath.

[8] Ghoul L357
(HPL: Selected Letters II) In 1948, Arthur C. Clarke sent Lord Dunsany a copy of The Arkham Sampler containing part of The Dream-Quest. Dunsany responded: "I see Lovecraft borrowed my style, & I don't grudge it to him". Connections to other Lovecraft tales[] The ghoul Richard Upton Pickman first appeared in "Pickman's Model" (1927) in which he is still human and painting nightmare creatures he calls forth as models. The priest Atal appears as a boy and youth in two earlier tales, "The Cats of Ulthar" (1920) and "The Other Gods" (1933), respectively, which fully describe events alluded to in The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath. Nyarlathotep, the Crawling Chaos, is frequently mentioned in Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos tales, but his appearance here is the only time he interacts meaningfully with any of Lovecraft's characters.

[9] Ghouls L393
Kadath is also briefly mentioned in At the Mountains of Madness. The Sign of Koth is mentioned in The Case of Charles Dexter Ward as inscribed on a tower in the dreamworld (to keep the gugs from returning to upper dreamland) and as having strange attributes. It is also inscribed in the catacombs under Curwen's long abandoned house. Neither novelette was published in Lovecraft's lifetime. --- The_Outsider_The_H.P._Lovecraft_Wiki_Fandom_e0cf9d3090.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L293
God knows it was not of this world — or no longer of this world — yet to my horror I saw in its eaten-away and bone-revealing outlines a leering, abhorrent travesty of the human shape; and in its mouldy, disintegrating apparel an unspeakable quality that chilled me even more. " In his shock and surprise, he loses his balance and touches the creature. Horrified, he runs from the building back to his castle, where he tries unsuccessfully to crawl back through the grate into his old world. Cast out of his old existence, the narrator now rides with the "mocking and friendly ghouls on the night wind," forever and officially an outsider since the moment he stretched his fingers towards the creature in the darkness and felt nothing but the "cold and unyielding surface of polished glass," signifying he had touched a mirror. Prior to telling of how he discovered that the monster was, in fact, himself, the narrator explains that he fled to a valley of the Nile in Egypt, where he exists alongside other outsiders - presumably undead, like himself - and even enjoys something of a social life (for example, a feast beneath one of the Pyramids), although he describes how "nepenthe has calmed me", hinting that he is still trying to forget his haunted past. Analysis[] Horror historian Les Daniels described "The Outsider" as "arguably the author's finest work".

[2] Ghouls L323
Kelly Hurley writes that the "abhuman subject is a not-quite-human subject, characterized by its morphic variability, continually in danger of becoming not-itself, becoming other." The idea of "becoming other" parallels what is happening in this story. The intensity of the process is heightened because the reader is learning of this transition from human to the abhuman right along with the narrator, who is learning it himself. Continuity[] Ghouls make frequent appearances in Lovecraft's work, although they are generally very different from the undead creatures described here. (HPL: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath) Nitocris makes an appearance in HPL: "Imprisoned with the Pharaohs" and ADJ: "The Queen's Enemies" [Lord Dunsany] Nephren-Ka is the Pharaoh who built "a temple with a windowless crypt" to the Shining Trapezohedron, and "did that which caused his name to be stricken from all monuments and records". --- The_Rats_in_the_Walls_The_H.P._Lovecraft_Wiki_Fandom_73fd7e38f8.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L259
(HPL: commonplace book 79) Steven J. Mariconda points to Sabine Baring-Gould's Curious Myths of the Middle Ages (1862—68) as a source for Lovecraft's story. The description of the cavern under the priory has many similarities to Baring-Gould's account of St. Patrick's Purgatory, a legendary Irish holy site, and the story of the priory's rats sweeping across the landscape may have been inspired by the book's retelling of the legend of Bishop Hatto, who was devoured by rats after he set fire to starving peasants during a famine. (EXP: "Baring-Gould and the Ghouls", The Horror of It All) See the story of the Mouse Tower of Bingen. Parts of Lovecraft's story bear a striking resemblance to Carl Jung's famous "house" dream (told to Sigmund Freud in 1909, though not well known before 1925): the descent through one's historically-stratified ancestral family home to a Romanesque cellar; lifting a hidden slab; descending stone steps to a prehistoric cave littered with bones, broken pottery, etc.

--- To Mars and Providence.txt ---

[1] Ghoul L109
At night, Howard sneaks out and enters the church, where he finds a shining trapezohedron The Martians, Howard learns, are descended from the same ancestral species that colonised both Mars and Earth, the latter in Antarctica , but evolved in a completely different direction by modifying their bodies and their brains. They eliminated all their emotions except for fear (as the latter was deemed necessary for survival) and built an advanced civilisation, making contact with a fungoid species from a world at the outskirts of the solar system . Through them, the Martians discovered that they weren't the first species to settle on Mars, and eventually started to uncover artifacts of a mighty race of long-faced, ghoul -like creatures that they called the Elder Gods . Finding that the Elder Gods haven't died out, but are merely asleep, the Martians grew fearful of their return, and ultimately decided to abandon Mars and take over Earth, leaving the red planet to its dormant masters. The colour also informs Howard that some years ago, some Martians have sent their minds through space to inhabit human bodies and gather information about the Earth. While most of them have returned, a few experienced amnesia and are still living as humans.

[2] Ghoul L123
Sensing Howard's feelings of being an outsider among his own people, and knowing that his mind was strong enough to activate the trapezohedron, the colour asks him if he might be one of them. Howard considers the possibility, thinking of how his dreams of other worlds have always felt more real than his mundane life on Earth, and agrees to be mentally transported to Mars, where his mind will manifest itself in a physical shape reflecting his real nature. Howard expects to show up as a Martian and be welcomed by his peers, but instead finds that the Martians are scared of him, as a look at a mirror reveals him to be one of the ghoul-like Elder Gods. The shock sends Howard's consciousness back to his body on Earth, and makes him forget all of the adventure. War of the Worlds: Global Dispatches (1996) Eternal Lovecraft: The Persistence of H. P. Lovecraft in Popular Culture (1998) Through Dark Angles: Works Inspired by H. P. Lovecraft (2014) Trivia "To Mars and Providence" contains numerous references to Lovecraft's works. Notably, the last eight words are the same as the ones from " The Outsider

--- Tsan-Chan.txt ---

[1] Ghouls L95
In this interpretation, it is an empire which rules what used to be China and Korea, plus great parts of Thailand, Vietnam, and Myanmar. Tsan Chan is not a Chinese empire but it does exist as if it was a fever dream of ancient China. The architecture is similar to that of ancient China, and so are the fashions and diet. The language has drifted due to mixing with other groups and the naming conventions are to a degree Chinese. The empire prosecuted several wars against the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos , including the Tcho-Tcho people and the Star Spawn , and have made such diverse allies as the Ghouls and Tsathoggua Using Deathless and Serpent magic in conjunction with the technology of the Elder Things , the Tsan Chang suceeded in forging a more powerful and effective Interdiction (a form of enormous Elder Sign ), turning it into a colossal wall which surrounds the empire. God-Trap technology warns away those powerful predator races of the Mythos. Dreamers and Tcho-Tcho are kept away by mine-fields, barbed wire, and gun turret emplacements. Weapons that employ the technology of the Elder Things includes beam cannons that fire an invisible beam which creates an Elder Sign, lethal toward Mythos creatures. The Mighty Children which survived the war became the Empire's nobility, it's new rulers. To prevent them from summoning their parents and other entities to the Earth, the Serpents closed every interdimensional and interplanetary portal within the empire.

On his first night's watch, Kearney tackles a strange creature resembling those in the paintings which is trying to enter the gallery, although it runs off after being shot. Meanwhile, Balmer receives the first of a series of phone calls threatening him with death if he does not destroy the paintings.
